rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-3 - the study builds and calibrates a hydraulic model (EPANET/HuraGIS) of the Senyera WUA with pressure sensors and flow meters, runs a genetic algorithm over 12 sectoring scenarios and reports predicted energy consumption and cost (Tables 4-9).
rows.notes: The study's own results concern energy consumption and cost of pump units under different intake groupings with fixed 2-h irrigation periods (predicted savings up to 36.4%, Table 8). It does not measure or model water applied per plot against crop water requirements, nor report any result on over- or under-irrigation or water management efficiency arising from uniform scheduled irrigation times. The passage's claim about inefficient water management is the citing review's inference, not a finding of this study.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3 - own calibrated hydraulic model of a real WUA (relative pressure error +2.8%, daily energy error +0.05% vs billing) and GA optimisation runs across 12 scenarios reported in Tables 6-9.
rows.notes: The passage describes an improved method (from the citing review) in which intakes are not restricted to fixed periods so crop water requirements are met more efficiently. In this study intakes are restricted to fixed 2-h sector periods and the only outcome evaluated is pumping energy and cost; crop water requirement satisfaction or water-use efficiency is neither measured nor modelled. Hence no own evidence on the claimed water-conservation effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is an energy-optimisation modelling case study (one WUA in Valencia, Spain) with model calibration against measured pressures and billed energy; it contains no evaluation of water application relative to crop needs, so neither claim about water management efficiency is supported by the study's own results.
